questions.prompt: Sort each part of Earth into the one system it mainly belongs to.
questions.accessiblePrompt: Sort eight parts of Earth into the one system each mainly belongs to: the geosphere, the hydrosphere, the atmosphere, or the biosphere. The parts are magma deep under Iceland, iron and nickel at Earth's center, groundwater filling cracks in rock, ice in an Arctic glacier, nitrogen gas in the air, thin air high over the clouds, a polar bear, and mushrooms breaking down a fallen log.

items.text: Magma deep under Iceland
items.rationale: Geosphere: magma is melted rock inside Earth, still part of the planet's rock material.

items.text: Iron and nickel at Earth's center
items.rationale: Geosphere: the core is the innermost layer of the geosphere, even though it is mostly metal.

items.text: Groundwater filling cracks in rock
items.rationale: Hydrosphere: it sits underground, but it is water, and the hydrosphere includes water wherever it is found.

items.text: Ice in an Arctic glacier
items.rationale: Hydrosphere: frozen water is still water, and the hydrosphere includes ice wherever it is found.

items.text: Nitrogen gas in the air
items.rationale: Atmosphere: nitrogen is the most common gas in the air.

items.text: Thin air high over the clouds
items.rationale: Atmosphere: the air thins out with height, but it is still part of the gas envelope around Earth.

items.text: A polar bear
items.rationale: Biosphere: it is a living thing, even though it spends its days on sea ice.

items.text: Mushrooms breaking down a fallen log
items.rationale: Biosphere: decomposers such as mushrooms are living things too.

questions.explanation: Sort by what each thing is. Rock and metal, like magma and the core, are geosphere. Water in any form or place, like groundwater and glacier ice, is hydrosphere. Gases are atmosphere, and living things are biosphere. Being underground does not decide the system.
questions.misconception: Anything underground belongs to the geosphere, and frozen water is not part of the hydrosphere.
questions.hint: Ask what each thing is (rock or metal, water, a gas, or something alive), not where it happens to be.

questions.prompt: A chunk of mantle rock is heated and expands slightly. Its mass stays the same. What happens to its density?

choices.text: It increases, because hot rock packs its particles tighter

questions.prompt: A parcel of rock near the top of the mantle has a mass of 3,300 g and a volume of 1,000 cm³, the same density as the rock around it. It loses energy and contracts to 990 cm³, while its mass stays 3,300 g. What is its new density, to two decimal places?
questions.accessiblePrompt: A parcel of rock near the top of the mantle has a mass of 3,300 grams and a volume of 1,000 cubic centimeters, the same density as the rock around it. It loses energy and contracts to 990 cubic centimeters, while its mass stays 3,300 grams. What is its new density in grams per cubic centimeter, rounded to two decimal places?
questions.workedSolution: Density = mass ÷ volume. Before: 3,300 g ÷ 1,000 cm³ = 3.30 g/cm³. After cooling: 3,300 g ÷ 990 cm³ = 3.333… g/cm³, which rounds to 3.33 g/cm³.
questions.explanation: The cooled parcel is now slightly denser (3.33 g/cm³) than the rock around it (3.30 g/cm³), so gravity pulls it down. That is the sinking half of a mantle convection cell; warming does the opposite.
questions.misconception: A tiny change in volume can't change density enough to matter.
questions.hint: Divide the mass by the new volume, not the old one.

evidence.supports: Density is mass per volume; when rock cools it becomes denser, and gravity makes cooler, denser rock sink in a convection cell while heated, less dense rock rises.

questions.prompt: A clear pot of room-temperature water is heated gently from below. The warmer water near the bottom starts to rise. Why can the warmer water rise?
questions.accessiblePrompt: A clear pot of room-temperature water is heated gently at the bottom. The warmer water near the bottom of the pot starts to rise. Why can the warmer water rise?

choices.text: It becomes less dense than the cooler water around it
choices.rationale: Correct. Warming spreads the water out a little, so it is less dense. Gravity pulls the cooler, denser water down beside it, and that sinking water pushes the warm water up: convection.

choices.text: Heat is lighter than cold, so it floats up and drags the water
choices.rationale: Heat isn't a substance with weight. Energy spreads from warmer to cooler places in any direction; the water rises because of its lower density.

choices.text: Each water molecule loses mass as it warms up
choices.rationale: Warming doesn't change a molecule's mass. The molecules spread farther apart, which lowers the density of the water as a whole.

choices.text: Rising air bubbles carry the warm water upward
choices.rationale: Gentle heating makes few bubbles, and they can't haul the water along. Warm water rises even when there are no bubbles at all.

questions.explanation: Warm water rises because it is less dense than the cooler water around it. Gravity pulls the denser, cooler water down, which pushes the warmer water up; near the top the water cools, becomes denser and sinks again. That density-driven circulation is convection.
questions.misconception: Heat itself rises, or warm water molecules become lighter.
questions.hint: Compare how tightly packed the warm water is with the cooler water beside it.

evidence.locator: Introduction vocabulary and Section 1. Energy and the Cycling of Matter in the Geosphere
evidence.supports: Convection is energy transfer caused by matter circulating because of density differences; heated material becomes less dense and rises while cooler, denser material sinks.

items.text: It slowly rises toward the crust

questions.prompt: Convection in the mantle, the ocean and the air needs two ingredients: differences in density (usually from uneven heating) and gravity. What job does gravity do in a convection cell?
questions.accessiblePrompt: Convection in Earth's mantle, in the ocean, and in the air needs two ingredients: differences in density, which usually come from uneven heating, and gravity. What job does gravity do in a convection cell?

choices.text: It pulls denser material down, pushing less dense material up
choices.rationale: Correct. Gravity pulls on all matter, but harder on each cubic meter of denser material, so cooler, denser material sinks and pushes warmer, less dense material up.

choices.text: It pulls the warmest material upward, away from Earth's center
choices.rationale: Gravity always pulls toward Earth's center. Warm material rises only because denser material sinks around it.

choices.text: It supplies the energy that warms the material at the bottom
choices.rationale: In these convection cells the warming comes from the sun or from Earth's hot interior. Gravity's job is to pull harder on denser material, not to warm it.

choices.text: Nothing; temperature differences alone keep the material moving
choices.rationale: Without gravity nothing would make denser material sink, so the loop would stall. Temperature differences only create the density differences that gravity acts on.

questions.explanation: Differences in density, usually from uneven heating, set the stage; gravity does the moving. It pulls harder on each cubic meter of denser material, and that squeezes less dense material up. The same pull is why magma, less dense than the rock around it, works its way toward volcanoes.

questions.prompt: Sort each example by how energy is being transferred: conduction, convection, or radiation.
questions.accessiblePrompt: Sort seven examples into three groups by how energy is being transferred: conduction, convection, or radiation. The examples are sunlight crossing empty space to reach Earth; sunlight passing through clear air and warming a dark rock; frigid polar air chilling the sea surface it touches; heat passing from the hot core into the mantle rock resting on it; warm air rising at the equator while cooler air sinks elsewhere; a cold, deep current creeping from the poles toward the equator; and sun-warmed sand heating your bare feet.

items.text: Sunlight crossing empty space to reach Earth
items.rationale: Radiation: space has too little matter for conduction or convection, so the energy travels as light.

items.text: Sunlight passing through clear air and warming a dark rock
items.rationale: Radiation: light carries the energy through the transparent air to the rock.

items.text: Frigid polar air chilling the sea surface it touches
items.rationale: Conduction: the air and water are in contact, and energy passes from the warmer water to the colder air.

items.text: Heat passing from the hot core into the mantle rock resting on it
items.rationale: Conduction: the core and the bottom of the mantle touch, so energy flows from the hotter material to the cooler one.

items.text: Warm air rising at the equator while cooler air sinks elsewhere
items.rationale: Convection: the air itself circulates, carrying energy as warm air rises and cool air sinks.

items.text: A cold, deep current creeping from the poles toward the equator
items.rationale: Convection: the water itself travels as part of the ocean's density-driven loop, carrying its energy with it.

items.text: Sun-warmed sand heating your bare feet
items.rationale: Conduction: the sun warmed the sand earlier, but the transfer here is from the hot sand into the cooler feet touching it.

questions.explanation: Ask what carries the energy. If it passes between materials that touch, that's conduction. If the material itself circulates, warm parts rising and cool parts sinking, that's convection. If light carries it, even through empty space or clear air, that's radiation.
questions.misconception: Any heating counts as convection, anything involving the sun is radiation, or energy cannot cross empty space.
questions.hint: For each example, ask: are two things touching, is material flowing in a loop, or is light doing the carrying?

choices.text: It is chilled by the frigid air over it
choices.rationale: Correct. Contact with very cold air draws energy out of the water by conduction, and colder seawater is denser.

choices.text: It becomes saltier as sea ice forms nearby
choices.rationale: Correct. When seawater freezes, most of the salt is left behind in the water, and saltier water is denser.

choices.text: It soaks up sunshine during the long polar summer
choices.rationale: Warming would make the water less dense, not denser. And polar sunlight arrives at a low slant, so it delivers little energy to each square meter.

choices.rationale: Correct. The warm air is less dense than the cooler air around it, so it rises. High up and farther from the equator it cools, becomes denser and sinks back toward the surface.

choices.rationale: As the air rises it cools and becomes denser, and gravity brings it back down. That return trip is what closes the loop of a convection cell.

questions.explanation: Warm air near the equator is less dense than the cooler air around it, so it rises. High up and farther from the equator it cools, becomes denser and sinks back toward the ground, ready to be heated once more. These loops of rising and sinking air are the atmosphere's convection cells, and they keep air and energy circulating around the globe.

evidence.locator: Section 3. The Atmosphere, Energy and the Cycling of Matter in the Atmosphere, and Figure 3 (Convection in the Atmosphere)
evidence.supports: Concentrated solar energy at the equator warms the air there and makes it less dense; the warmer air rises and moves away from the equator, cools at high altitude, becomes denser and sinks to the surface, where it can be warmed again. Figure 3 labels warmer, less dense air rising and cooler, denser air sinking in convection cells around the globe.

evidence.title: Climate and Earth's Energy Budget
evidence.supports: The atmosphere absorbs about 23 percent of incoming sunlight and the surface about 48 percent; the surface then passes energy to the atmosphere by evaporation, convection and thermal infrared radiation, so much of the atmosphere's energy comes from the surface below.

questions.conditions: Uses the lesson's simplified model of one air convection cell next to the equator.
questions.limitations: Simplified model: Figure 3 shows several convection cells side by side between the equator and the poles, and real winds are messier than one neat loop.
